label: codifies
point: The court held that under 5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(8) a policy disagreement can be a protected disclosure of gross mismanagement only if a disinterested observer could conclude the agency erred in a way not debatable among reasonable people, and that no irrefragable proof is required.
change: The WPEA changed 'a violation' to 'any violation' in (b)(8), split (b)(9)(A), added (b)(13) on nondisclosure agreements, and added a closing rule that the disinterested-observer test governs reasonable belief and that the presumption of official good faith may be rebutted by substantial evidence.
why: The committee report cites this decision approvingly for the rule that whistleblowers need not prove gross mismanagement by irrefragable proof, and the Act writes the disinterested-observer test from the same litigation (Lachance v. White) into the statute; nothing reverses White's treatment of policy disputes.

label: related
point: The court held that a VCAA notice error under 38 U.S.C. 5103(a) is presumed prejudicial, putting the burden on VA to show the error did not affect the fairness of the adjudication.
change: The Act renumbered 5103(a) as (a)(1) and added (a)(2) requiring VA to prescribe regulations on the contents of notice, varying by claim type.
why: The committee report names Sanders as a source of remand burdens, but the Act only standardizes notice content by regulation; it does not change the prejudicial-error rule or the burden the decision set.

label: unrelated
point: The court held that 18 U.S.C. 2515 and 2516 did not apply because the CIA copied stored e-mail rather than intercepting it in transmission.
change: The Act added National Security Division officials and many new predicate offenses to the list of crimes for which wiretap orders may be authorized.
why: Expanding the predicate-offense list has nothing to do with the decision's point that stored e-mail is not an interception.

label: unrelated
point: The Court held that sugar refined but not sent out of the manufactory before July 1, 1802 was not subject to duty after the internal taxes were repealed; it did not construe 23 U.S.C. 405.
change: No change to cited words was found; the matched passage in TEA-21 is a highway project list mentioning 'U.S. 34' (a highway), not the case.
why: The link is a false match on the citation '6 U.S. 34'; the highway law has no connection to an 1804 sugar-duty decision.

label: related
point: The court held that the Board had jurisdiction over the IRA appeal because Yunus non-frivolously alleged a protected disclosure under 2302(b)(8), and affirmed on the ground that the agency would have removed him anyway.
change: The WPEA changed 'a violation' to 'any violation' in (b)(8), split (b)(9)(A), added (b)(13), and added rules on the disinterested-observer test and rebutting the good-faith presumption.
why: The report cites Yunus only as an example of existing jurisdictional/procedural practice; the amendments broaden what counts as a protected disclosure but would not change the decision's jurisdictional holding or its clear-and-convincing-evidence result.

label: codifies
point: The Court held that the National Bank Act's visitorial-powers clause does not bar state attorneys general from enforcing non-preempted state law through judicial proceedings, citing 12 U.S.C. 481 only to describe the examiner provision.
change: In 481 the Act only made assessment fees subject to chapter 71 of title 5; separately it added a visitorial-powers provision expressly 'in accordance with' Cuomo v. Clearing House.
why: Dodd-Frank names this decision and writes its holding into the statute; the specific change to 481's fee language is unrelated to the decision's point.

label: override_express
point: The court held that a computerized database of Supreme Court decisions was library reference material and not an agency record under FOIA, and alternatively that an agency need not supply records in the requester's preferred (electronic) format.
change: The E-FOIA amendments added electronic reading-room and index duties and required agencies to provide records in any form or format requested if readily reproducible in that form or format.
why: The committee report names Baizer as following the Dismukes no-format-preference rule and as a reason to legislate on form and format, and the Act reverses that alternative ground; the primary library-reference holding is untouched, so the result would likely stand.

label: unrelated
point: The court applied the economic substance doctrine to deny losses from ACM's contingent-installment-sale tax shelter; 26 U.S.C. 1 was cited only generally.
change: The Act removed foreign investment company and foreign personal holding company references from the qualified-dividend rules in section 1(h).
why: The report names ACM only in describing the common-law economic substance doctrine (not codified in this Act), and the section 1 change concerns qualified-dividend definitions unrelated to the decision.

label: unrelated
point: The court held that gas qualified as tight formation gas for the section 29 credit only if a formal NGPA well-category determination was obtained; section 56 was not at issue.
change: The Act changed ACE earnings-and-profits adjustments in section 56(g) (replacing references to section 114 with 1357, adding rules for sections 199 and 965).
why: The ACE adjustment changes have nothing to do with the section 29 tight-formation holding, and the report names True v. United States (D. Wyo.), a different gathering-system depreciation case.

label: unrelated
point: The court held that the Rio player was not a digital audio recording device under the AHRA, citing the 17 U.S.C. 101 definition of literary works to show computer programs are fixed in material objects such as hard drives.
change: The Act added a definition of 'motion picture exhibition facility' to section 101.
why: The new definition (for the camcorder-piracy offense) has no bearing on the decision's reading of literary works, and the report's citation is to Huntsman v. Soderbergh, a different case mis-cited to the same reporter page.
